what: The score is the fixed-position insertion cost minus the cost of serving the candidate alone: Δ(c) − 2d(depot,c). Thus, minimizing it maximizes the immediate distance saving obtained by consolidating the candidate into the current route instead of retaining a singleton route. It uses only three insertion-edge distances and one depot distance, so each call is O(1) in time and space.
why: Pure cheapest insertion can favor inexpensive near-depot customers while leaving remote customers for later depot-to-depot trips. The singleton-saving term rewards candidates that are both remote and geometrically compatible with the current route; candidates on an incompatible side receive little consolidation saving because their insertion cost approaches their standalone cost. This tends to support spatially coherent routes, whose ordering can then be improved by 2-opt. The rule is scale-free with respect to coordinate units and needs no tuned instance-family constants. It remains a greedy proxy: it ignores demand packing beyond the caller's feasibility check, interactions among unassigned customers, and the exact changes that later insertions or 2-opt will produce, so no general improvement is guaranteed.
